tips.title: What is Antigravity?
tips.subtitle: Learn about the AI-powered coding assistant
tips.body:
# What is Antigravity?

Antigravity is an AI-powered coding assistant that runs directly inside your IDE and connects to your iOS device via the **PhiaManus** app.

## How It Works

1. **Install the extension** in VS Code or your preferred IDE
2. **Scan the QR code** displayed in the extension to pair your phone
3. **Send prompts** from the app to your AI assistant in the IDE

Your code context is automatically shared so the AI always knows what you're working on.

## Key Features

- 📱 Real-time sync between your phone and IDE
- 🔒 Secure local connection — your code never leaves your machine
- ⚡ One-tap prompt sending with full context
- 🎨 Customizable themes and prompt libraries

tips.title: Setting Up Your Workspace
tips.subtitle: Install Antigravity iOS App Connector in your IDE
tips.body:
# Setting Up Your Workspace

## Step 1: Install the Extension

Install the **Antigravity iOS Connector** extension from the VS Code marketplace.

```
ext install antigravity.phiamanus-connector
```

## Step 2: Start the Server

Open the Command Palette (`Cmd+Shift+P`) and run:

```
PhiaManus: Start Server
```

A QR code will appear in the status bar.

## Step 3: Pair Your Phone

Open PhiaManus on your phone, tap **Scan Pairing QR**, and point your camera at the QR code in VS Code.

✅ You'll see **Connected** appear in both the app and the IDE.

## Troubleshooting

- Make sure your phone and computer are on the **same WiFi network**
- Check that port `3000` is not blocked by a firewall
- Try the **Enter Code Manually** option if scanning doesn't work

tips.title: Your First Prompt
tips.subtitle: Send your first prompt from the app
tips.body:
# Sending Your First Prompt

## Using the Prompt Library

1. Tap **More → Prompts** in the app
2. Browse categories like *Architecture*, *Backend*, or *Testing*
3. Tap a prompt to see the full text
4. Tap **Send to IDE** to send it with your current file context

## Quick Send

You can also type a custom message directly in the IDE terminal and press Enter.

## Context Chips

The chips at the top of the workspace screen show which files are currently included as context. Tap the ✕ to remove one, or clear all at once.

> **Tip:** The more specific your context, the better the AI response. Try selecting only the files relevant to your current task.

tips.title: Writing Clear Prompts
tips.subtitle: How to communicate effectively with AI
tips.body:
# Writing Clear Prompts

The quality of the AI response depends heavily on the quality of your prompt. Here's how to write prompts that get great results.

## Be Specific About Outcome

❌ *"Fix this code"*

✅ *"Fix the null pointer exception in the `processPayment` function when `user` is undefined. Return an error object instead of throwing."*

## Include Constraints

Tell the AI what you **don't** want:

- *"Don't change the public API"*
- *"Use only the existing dependencies, don't add new ones"*
- *"Keep backward compatibility with Node 18"*

## Specify Output Format

- *"Show a diff"*
- *"Explain the changes in bullet points after the code"*
- *"Output only the changed function, not the whole file"*

## Golden Rule

> If you wouldn't understand your request without extra context, neither will the AI.

tips.title: Using Context Effectively
tips.subtitle: Help AI understand your codebase
tips.body:
# Using Context Effectively

PhiaManus sends your current file context with every prompt. Here's how to use this power wisely.

## What Gets Sent

- The currently **open files** in your IDE
- The **file tree** structure of your workspace
- Any **context chips** you've explicitly added

## Context Tips

### Focus the Context
Close files that aren't relevant. Open only the files the AI needs to understand the problem.

### Use Context Chips
Tap the **+** in the workspace screen to pin specific files as persistent context. Useful for:
- Shared types/interfaces
- Configuration files
- Related service files

### Be Explicit About Files
Mention the filename in your prompt:

> *"In `UserService.ts`, refactor the `getUser` method to use the repository pattern shown in `UserRepository.ts`"*

## Large Codebases

For large projects, use the file tree in the app to navigate and add context chips for only the relevant modules.

tips.title: Choosing the Right Prompt
tips.subtitle: When to use different prompt types
tips.body:
# Choosing the Right Prompt

Different tasks call for different prompt strategies.

## Task-Based Prompts
Best for: *"Do X to my code"*

Examples from the Prompts library:
- **Code Review Expert** — thorough review with severity ratings
- **Unit Test Generator** — create tests for your functions
- **Optimize This Code** — improve performance and readability

## Explain Prompts
Best for: *"Help me understand X"*

- **Explain Like I'm Junior** — plain-language explanations
- **Bug Investigation** — systematic debugging approach

## Architecture Prompts
Best for: *"Design how to do X"*

- **Architecture Decision Record** — document decisions
- **Microservice Boundaries** — define service boundaries
- **Design Pattern Advisor** — get pattern recommendations

## Custom Prompts

Don't see what you need? Tap **Add Custom Prompt** in the Prompts screen to create your own reusable prompt with title, tags, and body text.

tips.title: What are MCPs?
tips.subtitle: Understanding Model Context Protocol
tips.body:
# What are MCPs?

**MCP** stands for **Model Context Protocol** — an open standard that allows AI models to connect to external tools and data sources.

## Think of MCPs as Plugins

MCPs extend your AI assistant with new capabilities:

| MCP | What It Does |
|---|---|
| `filesystem` | Read/write files on your machine |
| `github` | Query repos, PRs, and issues |
| `postgres` | Run SQL queries on your database |
| `brave-search` | Search the web in real-time |

## How to Install an MCP

1. Find an MCP in the **Extensions** screen
2. Copy the installation command
3. Run it in your IDE terminal or add to your IDE config

## Where MCPs Live

MCPs run as local processes on your machine. Your AI communicates with them over a standard protocol, keeping your data secure.

> **Note:** Gemini CLI manages MCP connections through its skills system. See the Extensions screen for a curated list.

tips.title: Essential MCPs for Workflow
tips.subtitle: Must-have MCPs for your projects
tips.body:
# Essential MCPs for Workflow

These MCPs dramatically improve your AI coding experience.

## Tier 1: Must Have

### superpowers
```
gemini skills install obra/superpowers
```
Core TDD, debugging, and collaboration patterns. Start here.

### context7
```
gemini skills install upstash/context7
```
Up-to-date code documentation for any library, fetched on demand.

## Tier 2: Highly Recommended

### Sequential Thinking
Makes the AI think step-by-step before responding. Dramatically improves complex problem solving.

### Memory
Gives the AI persistent memory across sessions. It remembers your preferences, project conventions, and past decisions.

## Tier 3: Situational

| MCP | When to Use |
|---|---|
| `playwright` | Browser automation and E2E tests |
| `github` | Working with PRs and issues |
| `postgres` | Database-heavy development |
| `docker` | Container management |

> **Pro tip:** Start with just `superpowers` and add more as you identify specific gaps in your workflow.

tips.title: IDE Rules Files
tips.subtitle: Customize AI behavior with rules
tips.body:
# IDE Rules Files

Rules files let you set persistent instructions that apply to every AI interaction in your project.

## Where to Put Them

| File | Scope |
|---|---|
| `.gemini/GEMINI.md` | Gemini CLI |
| `.cursor/rules` | Cursor IDE |
| `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | GitHub Copilot |
| `CLAUDE.md` | Claude AI |

## What to Put in a Rules File

```markdown
# Project Rules

## Code Style
- Use TypeScript strict mode
- Prefer `const` over `let`
- Use early returns to reduce nesting

## Architecture
- Follow Clean Architecture layers
- Services go in `/src/services/`
- No business logic in controllers

## Testing
- Jest for unit tests
- All new functions need tests
- Mock all external dependencies
```

## Pro Tips

- Keep rules **concise** — long rules files reduce effectiveness
- Focus on **project-specific** conventions the AI wouldn't know
- Review and **update rules** as your project evolves
- Include your **tech stack** and **key dependencies**

tips.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
tips.subtitle: Speed up your workflow
tips.body:
# Keyboard Shortcuts

Master these shortcuts to stay in flow.

## Gemini CLI

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl+Y` | Accept suggestion |
| `Ctrl+N` | Next suggestion |
| `Esc` | Cancel current generation |
| `@filename` | Reference a specific file |
| `#symbol` | Reference a code symbol |

## VS Code + Extension

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Cmd+Shift+P` | Open command palette |
| `PhiaManus: Start` | Start the pairing server |
| `PhiaManus: Stop` | Stop the server |

## App Shortcuts

- **Pull down** on the Prompts list to refresh sources
- **Long press** a prompt to copy the text directly
- **Swipe left** on a custom prompt to delete it

## Pro Tip: Custom Snippets

Save your most-used prompt fragments as custom prompts in the app. One tap sends the full context — no typing required.

tips.title: Composer Best Practices
tips.subtitle: Build features with multiple components
tips.body:
# Composer Best Practices

When building multi-file features with AI assistance, these practices prevent common pitfalls.

## Plan Before You Code

Before asking the AI to write code, describe the full feature:

> *"I'm adding a user authentication system. It needs: a login screen, a JWT service, a user repository, and auth middleware. Start with the interfaces and types."*

## Work in Layers

1. **Types/Interfaces first** — define the data shapes
2. **Core logic** — business rules without dependencies
3. **Data layer** — repositories and services
4. **UI layer** — components that use the services
5. **Tests** — write tests for each layer

## Review Each Step

Don't ask for the whole feature at once. Review and approve each layer before moving to the next.

## Keep Changes Small

> *"Now add just the `login` endpoint to the auth controller. Don't touch the existing endpoints."*

Small, focused changes are easier to review, test, and roll back.

## Commit Frequently

Commit working code after each layer. This gives you a fallback if something goes wrong later.
